name: D1.0 The basic words of cybersecurity

paragraphes: Your phone holds your photos and your messages. You lock it with a code.
Without knowing it, you already do security. You protect what matters to you.
A company does the same, but with thousands of devices and files. Keeping all of that safe is called cybersecurity, or information security.

decouverte.comme: A house is not safe with just a door. It also has a lock, an alarm, and neighbors who look out.
decouverte.enVrai: Cybersecurity also mixes three things: people, rules, and tools. Rules are written instructions that tell people what to do. A tool is a program or a machine that helps to protect, like a lock. One of the three alone is not enough.

decouverte.question: In a company, who is responsible for security?
options: Only the IT team
Only the boss
Everyone in the company
decouverte.explanation: Security is everyone's job. One mistake by one worker can cause a big problem. The other answers are tempting because many people think security is only for experts.

decouverte.titre: The CISSP, a diploma for security
decouverte.texte: The CISSP is a certification. It is like a respected diploma that shows you know information security well. A group called (ISC)2 gives it. To keep it, you must follow rules of good conduct.

decouverte.comme: To visit a big country, you split it into regions. You visit them one by one.
decouverte.enVrai: The CISSP course is split into eight domains. A domain is a big topic. Domain 1 is about how to manage security in a company. Before that, you learn the basic words.

cards.question: What is cybersecurity?
options: Protecting only the machines, and not the information
Protecting only the building of the company
Protecting information and computers from harm
Making sure all the computers run very fast
options_why: The information on the machines is the real treasure. Cybersecurity protects both.
A locked building helps, but cybersecurity is about information and computers.
Speed helps people work, but it is not the same as protection.
cards.answer: Protecting information and computers from harm
cards.explanation: Cybersecurity means keeping information and computers safe. Think of the code on your phone.

cards.question: A company wants strong security. Which mix does it need?
options: People, rules, and tools together
The most expensive tools only
Written rules only, kept in a big book
Trained people only, with no tools
options_why: Tools can be used badly or passed by. People and rules close the other doors.
A rule that nobody follows protects nothing.
People cannot watch everything alone. They need tools to help them.
cards.answer: People, rules, and tools together
cards.explanation: Each part covers the weak points of the others. This is why a house has a door, a lock, and an alarm.

cards.question: Who plays a part in the security of a company?
options: Only the IT team, because they know computers
Only the managers, because they make decisions
Only the people who sign the security rules
Every worker in the company
options_why: The IT team leads, but any worker can cause a problem or stop one.
Managers set the direction, but everyone must follow the rules.
Rules apply to all workers, not only to the people who write them.
cards.answer: Every worker in the company
cards.explanation: Security is everyone's job. One worker can open the door by mistake, and one worker can raise the alarm.

cards.question: What is cybersecurity?
cards.answer: Protecting information and computers from unwanted access, changes, and breakdowns.
cards.explanation: Think of the code that locks your phone.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: protecting information and systems from inappropriate access, use, and change.

cards.question: A worker gets a strange message from a coworker. What should she do FIRST?
options: Delete the message and say nothing
Tell the security team about the strange message
Send it to friends to ask what they think
Open the message to see what it says
options_why: The problem stays, and other workers may get the same message.
This spreads the message and shares company information.
A strange message can be a trap. Opening it can make things worse.
cards.answer: Tell the security team about the strange message
cards.explanation: A quick report helps to limit the damage before it spreads. Everyone has a role in security.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: users must report any real or possible security problem.

cards.question: A company only bought new tools and did nothing else. What is the BEST way to make its security stronger?
options: Buy even more tools for the same job
Ask the IT team to do all the work alone
Wait for a problem and then fix it
Train workers and write clear rules
options_why: More tools do not fix people who use them badly.
Security is everyone's job, not only the job of one team.
Waiting is reactive. It is better to prevent a problem.
cards.answer: Train workers and write clear rules
cards.explanation: Tools are one part. People and rules are the other two parts. The three work together.

cards.question: Why is security everyone's job? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: One mistake by any worker can cause a problem. And any worker can stop a problem by telling the right people.
cards.explanation: Think of the worker who reports a strange message.

cards.question: Which of these is a rule, NOT a tool?
options: A written document that says who may enter the office
An alarm that rings if someone forces the door
An electronic lock on the office door
A camera that watches the hall
options_why: An alarm is a tool. It is a machine that helps to protect.
A lock is a tool. A rule would be the instruction about who may use it.
A camera is a tool. It records, but it does not tell people what to do.
cards.answer: A written document that says who may enter the office
cards.explanation: A rule is a written instruction. A tool is a machine or a program.

cards.question: A company has strong locks and alarms, but workers share their codes with friends. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: The tools are not strong enough
The company has too many locks
The people part is weak
The company has no tools at all
options_why: The locks and alarms are strong. The habit of sharing codes is the problem.
More locks do not fix a code that is shared.
It has locks and alarms, so it has tools.
cards.answer: The people part is weak
cards.explanation: Good tools can be passed when people do not follow good habits. Training and rules help.

cards.question: What is a rule in cybersecurity? Give an example.
cards.answer: A rule is a written instruction that tells people what to do. Example: lock your screen when you leave your desk.
cards.explanation: Rules are one of the three parts, with people and tools.

cards.question: How many domains does the CISSP course have?
options: Four
Eight
Six
Twelve
options_why: That is too few. The course has eight big topics.
Close, but the course has eight domains.
That is too many. There are eight domains.
cards.answer: Eight
cards.explanation: The CISSP course has eight domains. This course starts with domain 1.
cards.explanation_more: Source: outline of the (ISC)2 manual: eight domains.

cards.question: What does (ISC)2 do?
options: It sells security tools to companies
It writes the laws about company data
It checks the security of every company
It gives the CISSP certification
options_why: It does not sell tools. It gives certifications.
Laws come from the state. (ISC)2 sets rules for its own members.
It does not check companies. It tests and certifies people.
cards.answer: It gives the CISSP certification
cards.explanation: (ISC)2 is the group behind the CISSP. A member who breaks its code of conduct can lose the certification.

cards.question: What is a tool in cybersecurity? Give an example.
cards.answer: A tool is a program or a machine that helps to protect. Example: a lock or an alarm.
cards.explanation: A tool alone is not enough. It needs people and rules.

cards.question: Information security and cybersecurity: how are they related?
options: They have almost the same goal
Cybersecurity is only about phones
Information security is only about paper files
They are opposite ideas
options_why: It covers all devices, not only phones.
It covers digital information too.
They both mean protecting information and the machines that hold it.
cards.answer: They have almost the same goal
cards.explanation: In this course you can treat the two names as the same idea. The CISSP manual mostly uses information security.

cards.question: Which sentence describes the CISSP MOST correctly?
options: A program that blocks attackers every day
A law about how companies keep data
A respected security certification
A tool that finds weak points in code
options_why: The CISSP is a diploma, not a program.
A law comes from the state. The CISSP comes from (ISC)2.
It proves what a person knows. It is not a tool.
cards.answer: A respected security certification
cards.explanation: A certification is a diploma that proves your skills.
cards.explanation_more: CISSP stands for Certified Information Systems Security Professional (outside the manual: the full name).

cards.question: What is the CISSP?
cards.answer: A respected certification in information security. It shows that you know the job well.
cards.explanation: It is given by a group called (ISC)2.

cards.question: Why is one protection never enough?
cards.answer: One protection can break or be passed. With several layers, the others still work.
cards.explanation: Think of a house: the door, the lock, and the alarm.

decouverte.titre: The phone that will not turn on
paragraphes: Your phone will not turn on. Maybe the screen is broken. Or maybe a program is stuck.
In the first case, the problem is a part that you can touch. In the second, it is a part that you cannot touch.
The first is called hardware. The second is called software.

decouverte.titre: A piano and its sheet music
decouverte.comme: The piano is the object that you touch. The sheet music tells you which notes to play. Without the music, the piano is silent.
decouverte.enVrai: Hardware is the computer itself: the screen, the keyboard, and the parts inside. Software is the list of instructions that tells it what to do. A piece of software is also called a program. The image stops here: you can copy software with one click, but you cannot copy a piano.

decouverte.question: Is a video game hardware or software?
options: Hardware
Software
Both at the same time
decouverte.explanation: The game is a set of instructions, so it is software. The console that runs it is the hardware. Many people think the game is an object inside the console, but it is instructions.

decouverte.comme: In a restaurant kitchen, the head chef shares the work and checks that all goes well.
decouverte.enVrai: The operating system (OS) does this job inside a computer. Windows, macOS, and Linux are examples. It links the hardware and the applications. An application is a program made for one task, like a game or a calculator.

decouverte.titre: The customers of an online shop
decouverte.texte: An online shop saves the name, address, and orders of each customer. Each piece of saved information is data. A file is data saved under one name. Data that is stored in an organized way is a database. If someone changes the data by mistake, the shop sends the wrong package. A computer, its programs, and its data working together form a system.

cards.question: A laptop screen is cracked. What kind of problem is it?
options: A hardware problem
A software problem
A data problem
An operating system problem
options_why: The screen is a part that you can touch. Software is the instructions.
Data is the information. The screen only shows it.
The operating system is a program. It is not the glass of the screen.
cards.answer: A hardware problem
cards.explanation: You can touch a screen, so it is hardware.

cards.question: Which one of these is software?
options: The keyboard of a laptop
The disk that stores the files
The charger cable
A game on your phone
options_why: You can touch a keyboard, so it is hardware.
The disk is a part you can touch. It holds files, but it is not a program.
A cable is a part you can touch.
cards.answer: A game on your phone
cards.explanation: A game is a set of instructions. It is software.

cards.question: Which sentence describes an operating system?
options: A big set of data that is stored in an organized way
The software that links hardware and applications
A program that is made for one task, like a calculator
The screen and the keyboard of the computer
options_why: That is a database, not an operating system.
That is an application. The operating system runs under all applications.
Those are hardware. The operating system is software.
cards.answer: The software that links hardware and applications
cards.explanation: Think of the head chef: the operating system shares the work between hardware and applications.

cards.question: What is hardware?
cards.answer: Hardware is the part of a computer that you can touch. Examples: the screen, the keyboard, the disk.
cards.explanation: Hardware can break, be stolen, or be damaged.

cards.question: An online shop saves names, addresses, and orders in an organized way. What is the BEST word for this?
options: A database
An operating system
An application
A single file
options_why: The operating system is the main software of the computer, not a set of customers.
An application does a task. Here we talk about the data itself.
A file is one piece of data with one name. A database holds many records in order.
cards.answer: A database
cards.explanation: Data stored in an organized way, which you can search fast, is a database.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT software?
options: Linux
A spreadsheet program
A calculator app
A USB stick
options_why: Linux is an operating system, so it is software.
A spreadsheet program is an application, so it is software.
An app is a program, so it is software.
cards.answer: A USB stick
cards.explanation: A USB stick is an object that you can touch. It is hardware.

cards.question: What is software?
cards.answer: Software is a set of instructions that tells the computer what to do. It is also called a program.
cards.explanation: It has no shape: you can only copy it or delete it.

cards.question: Which pair is a hardware example and then a software example?
options: A word processor, then the keyboard
A game, then Windows
A keyboard, then a word processor
A screen, then a disk
options_why: These are in the wrong order. A word processor is software.
Both of these are software.
Both of these are hardware.
cards.answer: A keyboard, then a word processor
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: can I touch it? If yes, it is hardware. If it gives instructions, it is software.

cards.question: An online shop changes a price in its database by mistake. What is the MOST likely result?
options: The screens of the shop stop working
Customers may pay the wrong amount of money
The operating system is deleted
Nothing, because data is not important
options_why: A wrong price is a data problem. Screens are hardware.
Changing one price does not remove the operating system.
Data is often the most valuable part. Wrong data leads to bad decisions.
cards.answer: Customers may pay the wrong amount of money
cards.explanation: The company relies on its data to act. If the data is wrong, its actions are wrong.

cards.question: What is data?
cards.answer: Data is information that is saved in a computer. Examples: a name, a photo, a number.
cards.explanation: For security, data is often the thing with the most value.

cards.question: A company uses Windows, macOS, and Linux. Which statement is MOST correct?
options: All three are operating systems, and all need protection
Only Windows needs protection
They are applications, so the IT team can ignore them
They are hardware, so locks are enough
options_why: Every operating system can have weak points.
They are operating systems, and the IT team must protect them.
They are software. Locks cannot protect software.
cards.answer: All three are operating systems, and all need protection
cards.explanation: A company that uses several systems must protect all of them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on technology: Windows, macOS, and Linux.

cards.question: Which one of these is data?
options: The keyboard used to type it
The browser that shows the form
The laptop that holds the form
A birth date that is typed in a form
options_why: The keyboard is hardware.
The browser is an application.
The laptop is hardware.
cards.answer: A birth date that is typed in a form
cards.explanation: A birth date describes a person. It is information, so it is data.

cards.question: What is an operating system (OS)?
cards.answer: The main software of a computer. It links the hardware and the applications. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux.
cards.explanation: Without it, applications could not use the hardware.

cards.question: A calculator app on a phone is an example of what?
options: Hardware
An application
An operating system
A database
options_why: You cannot touch the app. You can only touch the phone.
The operating system runs the apps. A calculator is one app.
A database is stored data. A calculator is a program.
cards.answer: An application
cards.explanation: An application is software made for one task.

cards.question: Which example is the BEST description of a system?
options: A single scanner that reads the price codes at the till
A file with the list of products
A checkout with its screen, scanner, and program
The program that adds the prices
options_why: A scanner is only one hardware part.
A file is data. A system joins hardware, software, and data.
A program is one part. A system has all the parts working together.
cards.answer: A checkout with its screen, scanner, and program
cards.explanation: A system is hardware and software that work together. When you protect a system, you protect all of its parts.

cards.question: What is a database?
cards.answer: A database is a large set of data that is stored in an organized way. Example: the customers of an online shop.
cards.explanation: You can search, add, or change a piece of data very fast.

cards.question: What is an application?
cards.answer: An application is software made for one task. Examples: a game, a messaging tool, a calculator.
cards.explanation: On a phone, people often say an app.

paragraphes: You send a message to a friend on the other side of the world. It arrives in a few seconds.
Your phones are not joined by one direct wire. Between you, there is a huge web of cables and machines.
Devices that are linked to share data form a network.

decouverte.comme: Roads link cities. Cars carry people and packages from one place to another.
decouverte.enVrai: A network links computers. Data travels like the cars. The internet is the worldwide network: millions of networks linked together.

decouverte.question: When you open a website, where are its pages kept?
options: Inside your phone
On a powerful computer, somewhere in the world
Inside your home internet box
decouverte.answer: On a powerful computer, somewhere in the world
decouverte.explanation: The pages are kept on a computer that is always on and answers all requests. It is called a server. Your phone only shows the pages, and your box only connects you.

decouverte.comme: You do not keep everything at home. You rent a space in a storage unit, and you pay for what you use.
decouverte.enVrai: Cloud computing means renting servers from a company. That company is a cloud provider. The servers are kept in big buildings called datacenters. The cloud is not in the sky. It is real machines.

decouverte.texte: In an office, workers share files on a server. Some of their tools run in the cloud. A company called an internet service provider (ISP) connects the office to the internet. When the ISP has a problem, the workers cannot use the cloud tools.

decouverte.comme: A road is open to everyone. A covered tunnel hides the cars inside it.
decouverte.enVrai: A virtual private network (VPN) is a safe tunnel through the internet. It links your device to a far network and hides the data inside. A worker at home can use it to reach the office network.

cards.question: What is the internet?
options: One huge computer in a datacenter
The software that runs on every phone
A company that sells connections to homes
A worldwide network of networks
options_why: The internet is not one machine. It is many networks joined together.
That is an operating system. The internet is a network.
That is an ISP. The internet is the network itself.
cards.answer: A worldwide network of networks
cards.explanation: The internet is the network of networks. A device that is on the internet can be reached from all over the world.

cards.question: Which one is a server?
options: A cable that joins two rooms of a building
A computer that answers requests all day
A screen that shows a website to a visitor
A phone app that opens many web pages at once
options_why: A cable is a part of a network, but it does not answer requests.
A screen shows the page. The page is kept on a server.
An app asks for a page. The server sends the page.
cards.answer: A computer that answers requests all day
cards.explanation: A server answers the requests of other devices. It stays on day and night.

cards.question: What is the cloud?
options: A storage space inside your own computer
A very fast type of internet cable
Rented servers that you reach online
A program that comes with every phone
options_why: The cloud is far away. You reach it through the internet.
It is not a cable. It is servers that you rent.
It is not a program. It is real machines in datacenters.
cards.answer: Rented servers that you reach online
cards.explanation: The name sounds like the sky, but the cloud is real servers in real buildings.

cards.question: What is a network?
cards.answer: A network is a group of devices that are linked to share data. Example: the computers of a school.
cards.explanation: If one device on the network is attacked, the others can be hit too.

cards.question: A worker is at a cafe and needs the company files. What is the BEST way to connect?
options: Use a VPN
Use the cafe Wi-Fi with nothing else
Send the files to a personal phone first
Ask a friend to send the files by message
options_why: Other people on a public Wi-Fi may be able to listen. It needs extra protection.
The files then leave the control of the company.
A message does not protect the files, and a friend should not see them.
cards.answer: Use a VPN
cards.explanation: A VPN makes a protected tunnel between the worker and the company network.

cards.question: A datacenter has a power failure. Who is MOST likely to be affected?
options: Only the owner of the datacenter
Only people who live near the building
Every company that rents servers in that building
Nobody, because the data is in the cloud
options_why: Many customers rent the same servers, so many companies are hit.
The servers can be used from anywhere, so users far away lose them too.
The cloud is real machines. If they stop, the services stop.
cards.answer: Every company that rents servers in that building
cards.explanation: Many companies share the same servers. If the machines stop, all the customers lose their services.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: power failures, floods, and heat are threats for datacenters.

cards.question: What is a server?
cards.answer: A server is a computer that answers the requests of other devices. Example: the one that sends the pages of a website.
cards.explanation: It is always on, so it is an interesting target for attackers.

cards.question: Which statement about the cloud is NOT true?
options: It uses servers in datacenters
It works without any real machines
You can reach it through the internet
A company can rent it from a provider
options_why: This is true. The cloud is made of servers in big buildings.
This is true. You use the cloud over the internet.
This is true. Renting is how most companies use the cloud.
cards.answer: It works without any real machines
cards.explanation: The cloud is not magic. It is real machines in real buildings.

cards.question: Which sentence BEST describes an internet service provider (ISP)?
options: The company that stores your files on rented servers
The company that makes your phone or laptop
The company that writes the apps that you use
The company that connects you to the internet
options_why: That is a cloud provider. An ISP only gives the connection.
That company makes hardware, not the connection.
That company makes software, not the connection.
cards.answer: The company that connects you to the internet
cards.explanation: If your ISP goes down, your devices stay on but they cannot reach the internet.

cards.question: What is the cloud (cloud computing)?
cards.answer: Using servers that you rent from a company and reach through the internet. Example: keeping your photos online.
cards.explanation: It is not a cloud in the sky. It is real machines in real buildings.

cards.question: Is the internal network of a school the same as the internet?
options: No, it is one small network among many
Yes, every network is the internet
Yes, if it has more than 100 computers inside
Yes, but only if it has a server
options_why: The internet joins millions of networks. One network is only one part.
The size does not matter. The internet is the network of networks.
A server does not make a network become the internet.
cards.answer: No, it is one small network among many
cards.explanation: A small network may not even be linked to the internet.

cards.question: You type a web address and your request reaches your ISP. Which step comes NEXT?
options: The page shows on your screen now
It crosses the internet to a server
The server sends the page back to you
You type the address again
options_why: This is the last step. The page must travel first.
The server must first receive your request.
This is the first step, and it already happened.
cards.answer: It crosses the internet to a server
cards.explanation: The order is: you type, the ISP gets it, it crosses the internet, a server answers, the page appears.

cards.question: What is a datacenter?
cards.answer: A datacenter is a big building full of servers. It needs electricity, cooling, and a good connection.
cards.explanation: It holds a lot of data, so it must be protected from breakdowns, fire, and intruders.

cards.question: A company must stay online. Which choice has the LEAST risk if one internet connection stops?
options: One ISP with a very fast line
One ISP with a long contract
Two ISPs, so that one can take over
One very big server in the office
options_why: A fast line still stops if the ISP stops.
A long contract does not keep the connection alive.
A bigger server does not help if the connection is lost.
cards.answer: Two ISPs, so that one can take over
cards.explanation: A spare connection means one failure does not stop the work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: some companies use more than one internet provider.

cards.question: What does a VPN do?
options: It hides your data inside a safe tunnel
It makes the internet faster
It stores your files in a datacenter
It checks if a website is real
options_why: A VPN protects the data. It does not add speed.
That is the job of the cloud.
A VPN protects the road, not the website.
cards.answer: It hides your data inside a safe tunnel
cards.explanation: Data inside the tunnel is hidden from people who listen on the network.

cards.question: What is a virtual private network (VPN)?
cards.answer: A VPN is a safe tunnel through the internet. It links your device to a far network and hides the data inside.
cards.explanation: Example: working from home on your company network.

cards.question: What is an internet service provider (ISP)?
cards.answer: An ISP is the company that connects you to the internet. Example: the company behind the internet box at your home.
cards.explanation: If your ISP goes down, you lose the internet.

paragraphes: At the school gate, the guard looks at your card and lets you in. But he does not let you into the teachers room.
He did two things. First, he checked that you are really you. Then, he decided where you can go.
A computer does the same. You prove who you are, and then the system decides what you can do.

decouverte.comme: At school, each student has a locker with a name on it. The padlock opens only with your code.
decouverte.enVrai: An account is your own place in a system. The username tells who it belongs to. The password is the secret code that proves it is you.

decouverte.question: Someone uses your password. What does the system think?
options: That it is really you
That a stranger is trying to get in
That it must ask for a photo
decouverte.explanation: The system cannot see your face. It only sees the password. This is why a stolen password is so dangerous. The other answers are tempting, but the system cannot guess.

decouverte.titre: Two proofs are better than one
decouverte.comme: To open a safe, you sometimes need a key and a code. A thief with only the key cannot open it.
decouverte.enVrai: Authentication means proving who you are. Multifactor authentication (MFA) asks for two or more proofs, such as a password and a code sent to your phone. A stolen password is not enough any more.

decouverte.texte: In a company, an accountant can see the invoices. A technician can install programs. Access rights, also called permissions, say what each person can see or do. Giving these rights is called authorization. The administrator is the person with the widest rights on a system. Access control means all the ways that decide who can go where.

decouverte.titre: One ticket for the whole park
decouverte.comme: At a theme park, one ticket lets you enter many rides. You do not buy a new ticket for each ride.
decouverte.enVrai: Single sign-on (SSO) works the same way. You sign in once and reach many services. It is easy. But if someone steals that sign-in, many doors open at once.

cards.question: A student shows a card at the gate. Then the guard says which rooms the student may enter. Which step is authorization?
options: The guard saying which rooms are allowed
Looking at the photo on the student's card
Showing the card to the guard at the gate
Walking through the gate
options_why: Checking the photo proves who the student is. That is authentication.
Showing the card is the proof of identity. That is authentication.
Walking in is an action. It is not a decision about rights.
cards.answer: The guard saying which rooms are allowed
cards.explanation: Authentication proves who you are. Authorization decides what you can do.

cards.question: Which one of these must stay secret?
options: The username
The name of the website
The password
The number of accounts in the company
options_why: A username shows who an account belongs to. It is often known.
Everyone can see the name of a website.
This is not a secret that proves anything.
cards.answer: The password
cards.explanation: The password is the proof that you are the owner of the account. If it is shared, the proof is lost.

cards.question: A system asks for a password and then a code sent to your phone. What is this called?
options: Authorization of each user account
Multifactor authentication
Single sign-on for all services
Access rights for each user
options_why: Authorization decides what you can do, not who you are.
Single sign-on lets you sign in once for many services.
Access rights are the list of what an account can do.
cards.answer: Multifactor authentication
cards.explanation: Two different proofs: a secret you know and an object you have.

cards.question: What is authentication?
cards.answer: Authentication is the act of proving that you are who you say you are. Example: typing your password.
cards.explanation: Saying who you are is not enough. You must prove it.

cards.question: A worker's password was stolen. Which extra protection BEST helps to stop a thief from signing in?
options: Make the password a little longer each year
Change the username of every worker each week
Ask the worker to sign in more often
Ask for a second proof, like a phone code
options_why: A longer password helps a bit, but it is still one proof that can be stolen.
The username is not the secret. Changing it does not stop a thief.
Signing in more often gives thieves more chances.
cards.answer: Ask for a second proof, like a phone code
cards.explanation: A thief who knows the password does not have the phone.

cards.question: Tom moved from accounting to marketing, but he can still read the invoices. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Ask Tom to stop opening the invoices for now
Remove the access that Tom no longer needs
Give Tom a longer and stronger password
Wait for the yearly review of rights
options_why: A polite request is not a control. The access must be removed.
The password is not the problem. The extra rights are.
Waiting leaves the door open for months.
cards.answer: Remove the access that Tom no longer needs
cards.explanation: When someone changes jobs, you remove the rights that they no longer need.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: remove access that is no longer needed when an employee moves.

cards.question: What is authorization?
cards.answer: Authorization decides what you are allowed to do after you are identified. Example: reading a folder but not changing it.
cards.explanation: Being recognized does not give you every right.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a good way to protect an account?
options: Sharing the password with a coworker that you trust
Using a long password that is used nowhere else
Adding a second proof to the sign-in
Signing out of shared computers
options_why: This is good. A unique password limits the damage of a theft.
This is good. A thief needs more than the password.
This is good. The next person cannot use your account.
cards.answer: Sharing the password with a coworker that you trust
cards.explanation: A shared password cannot prove who did what. Passwords must never be shared.

cards.question: Which account is MOST valuable to an attacker?
options: An account that can only read a menu
A new account that was never used
An administrator account
A guest account for visitors
options_why: This account has almost no rights, so it gives little.
An unused account with few rights is less useful.
A guest account has very few rights.
cards.answer: An administrator account
cards.explanation: An administrator has the widest rights. This account must be protected first.

cards.question: What is multifactor authentication (MFA)?
cards.answer: It is authentication with two or more different proofs. Example: a password and a code sent to your phone.
cards.explanation: A thief who knows your password does not have your phone.

cards.question: Which example BEST shows authorization?
options: Typing your password into the sign-in page
Placing a finger on the reader of a door
Entering the code that was sent to your phone
Being allowed to read a folder but not to change it
options_why: Typing a password proves who you are. That is authentication.
A fingerprint proves who you are. That is authentication.
A code proves who you are. That is authentication.
cards.answer: Being allowed to read a folder but not to change it
cards.explanation: Authorization is about what you may do after you are recognized.

cards.question: What is the main risk of single sign-on?
options: If the sign-in is stolen, many doors open
Users must sign in more often
Each service needs a different new password
It cannot be used together with a password
options_why: It is the opposite. You sign in only once.
It is the opposite. One sign-in works for many services.
A password is often the first proof, with SSO.
cards.answer: If the sign-in is stolen, many doors open
cards.explanation: It is easy to use, but that one account becomes very valuable.

cards.question: What is single sign-on (SSO)?
cards.answer: SSO lets you sign in once to reach several services. Example: one account for email and documents.
cards.explanation: It is handy, but if that account is stolen, everything opens.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual (domain 1): a useful idea for the rest of the course.

cards.question: Why should each person have their own username?
options: So passwords can be shorter
So the company can tell who did what
So that the account can have more rights
So nobody needs a password
options_why: A username does not make a password stronger.
Rights depend on the job, not on the username.
A username says who you are. The password proves it.
cards.answer: So the company can tell who did what
cards.explanation: If two people share an account, nobody can tell who did what.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: PCI DSS requirement 8 asks for a unique ID for each person.

cards.question: Which one is an example of access control?
options: A cable that joins two computers in one room
A program that writes documents
A fan that cools a server room
A password that decides who can open a private file
options_why: A cable joins devices. It does not decide who can enter.
A word processor is an application, not a control.
A fan protects the hardware from heat. It does not decide who enters.
cards.answer: A password that decides who can open a private file
cards.explanation: Access control means all the ways that decide who can go where. A badge, a password, and access rights are examples.

cards.question: What are access rights (permissions)?
cards.answer: Access rights are the list of what an account can see or do. They are also called privileges.
cards.explanation: The more rights an account has, the more dangerous it is if it is stolen.

cards.question: What is an administrator?
cards.answer: An administrator is the person who manages a system and has the widest rights.
cards.explanation: Their account is very valuable, so it must be protected first.
cards.explanation_more: The manual also writes sysadmin, short for system administrator.

paragraphes: You pass a secret note to a friend in class. If the teacher catches it, she reads it. So you make a code: each letter becomes the next letter.
The teacher reads “Ifmmp” and understands nothing. Your friend goes back one letter and reads “Hello”.
Making a message unreadable is called encrypting. Making it readable again is called decrypting.

decouverte.comme: Your “one letter forward” code works only if the other person knows the rule. Without the rule, the note means nothing.
decouverte.enVrai: In real encryption, everyone knows the method. The secret is the key: a very long string of numbers and letters. Without the right key, the message stays unreadable.

decouverte.question: A thief catches an encrypted message. Can the thief read it without the key?
options: Yes, by reading it with care
No, it stays unreadable without the key
decouverte.answer: No, it stays unreadable without the key
decouverte.explanation: Good encryption makes the text impossible to understand. The thief has the message, but nothing to read it with. Looking at it for a long time changes nothing.

decouverte.texte: When you pay online, your card data travels encrypted. A thief who catches it on the way sees only strange text. Only the website of the shop has the key to read it. Text that anyone can read is called plaintext. Encrypted text is called ciphertext. A message sent “in the clear” has no protection at all.

decouverte.comme: A fingerprint identifies a person. If the person is different, the fingerprint is different.
decouverte.enVrai: A hash is a short code that is made from a file. If you change one letter in the file, the code changes a lot. So you can see that a file was changed. But you cannot get the file back from its hash.

cards.question: A message is changed so that nobody can read it without a key. What is this called?
options: Decrypting the message
Hashing the message
Encrypting
Copying the message
options_why: Decrypting is the opposite. It makes a message readable again.
A hash makes a short code from a file. You cannot get the file back.
Copying makes a second version. It does not hide anything.
cards.answer: Encrypting
cards.explanation: To encrypt means to make a message unreadable without the key.

cards.question: Which one is ciphertext?
options: Text that looks random after encryption
A message that anyone can read
A very long secret string of numbers
A short code that shows if a file changed
options_why: That is plaintext. Ciphertext is the result of encryption.
That is a key. It is used to encrypt or decrypt.
That is a hash. It is not an encrypted message.
cards.answer: Text that looks random after encryption
cards.explanation: Ciphertext is the encrypted result. Without the key, it is unreadable.

cards.question: What does the key do?
options: It hides the method from all other people
It makes the message much shorter to send
It checks if a file was changed
It lets the right person read the text
options_why: The method is known to everyone. Only the key is secret.
A key does not shrink a message.
That is the job of a hash.
cards.answer: It lets the right person read the text
cards.explanation: The method is public. All the secret is in the key.

cards.question: What does it mean to encrypt?
cards.answer: To encrypt means to change a message so that it is unreadable without the key. Example: your card data in an online payment.
cards.explanation: The message still exists, but nobody can read it without the key.

cards.question: A laptop full of customer files is stolen. What BEST makes the data useless to the thief?
options: Putting a password on the screen saver
Encrypting the data on the laptop
Hiding the files in a folder with a strange name
Changing the name of the laptop
options_why: A thief can take out the disk and copy the files.
A strange name does not stop anyone from opening the folder.
The name of the laptop does not protect the files.
cards.answer: Encrypting the data on the laptop
cards.explanation: Without the key, the content stays unreadable, even if the thief copies everything.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: forgetting to encrypt sensitive data is a human mistake that threatens secrecy.

cards.question: A worker sends a salary list by email without encrypting it. How does the list travel?
options: In the clear
Encrypted with a key
Decrypted on the way
Hashed into a short code
options_why: Encrypted means a key made the message unreadable. That did not happen here.
Decrypting is the act of making a message readable again.
A hash is a short code. It does not send the list.
cards.answer: In the clear
cards.explanation: Without encryption, anyone who catches the message can read it.

cards.question: What does it mean to decrypt?
cards.answer: To decrypt means to turn an encrypted message back into plaintext with the right key.
cards.explanation: It is the opposite of encrypting. Only the right receiver has the key.

cards.question: Which statement about a hash is NOT true?
options: It is a short code made from a file
If the file changes, the code changes
You can use it to get the file back
It helps to see that a file was changed
options_why: This is true. A hash is a short code.
This is true. Even one changed letter gives a new code.
This is true. You compare the codes.
cards.answer: You can use it to get the file back
cards.explanation: A hash cannot be turned back into the file. It is only used to compare.

cards.question: You want to hide the content of a message from a thief. Which tool is the BEST choice?
options: A hash
Encryption
A longer file name
A bigger network
options_why: A hash shows changes. It does not hide the content.
A name does not protect the content.
A bigger network gives the thief more places to listen.
cards.answer: Encryption
cards.explanation: Encryption hides the content. A hash only spots a change.

cards.question: What is an encryption key?
cards.answer: A key is a long string of numbers and letters that is used to encrypt or decrypt. It must stay secret.
cards.explanation: The method is known to everyone. All the secret is in the key.

cards.question: A thief gets the encryption key of a company. What should the company do FIRST?
options: Ask the thief to give the key back
Wait to see if the thief uses the key
Delete all the encrypted data
Replace the key and encrypt again
options_why: A thief will not give it back, and may already have copies.
Waiting leaves all the data open.
This destroys the data. It does not fix the problem.
cards.answer: Replace the key and encrypt again
cards.explanation: With the old key, the thief can read the data. A new key stops this.

cards.question: A company wants to know if a contract file was changed in secret. What can it compare?
options: The name of the file before and after
The date on the folder before and after
The hash of the file before and after the change
The key of the file before and after
options_why: A name can stay the same while the content changes.
The date of a folder does not show a change inside the file.
The key does not show if the content changed.
cards.answer: The hash of the file before and after the change
cards.explanation: If the file changes, its hash changes. Different hashes mean a different file.

cards.question: What is plaintext?
cards.answer: Plaintext is text that anyone can read. It has no protection.
cards.explanation: Sending data in plaintext means sending it in the clear.

cards.question: A password protects a computer. Why is it MOST helpful to also encrypt its files?
options: A thief can copy the files and skip the password
Encrypted files do not need any key to be read
Passwords never work
Encryption makes the computer faster
options_why: Encrypted files always need a key to be read.
Passwords work, but they are not enough alone.
Encryption protects data. It does not add speed.
cards.answer: A thief can copy the files and skip the password
cards.explanation: The password guards the door. Encryption protects the content, even if the door is passed.

cards.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: To read plaintext, you need the right key
To read ciphertext, you need the key
To make a hash, you need the right key
To send plaintext safely, you need a hash
options_why: Plaintext can be read by anyone.
A hash is made from the file. No key is needed.
A hash does not make plaintext safe.
cards.answer: To read ciphertext, you need the key
cards.explanation: Ciphertext is unreadable without the key.

cards.question: What is ciphertext?
cards.answer: Ciphertext is the result of encryption. It is unreadable without the key.
cards.explanation: Plaintext goes in, ciphertext comes out.

cards.question: What is a hash?
cards.answer: A hash is a short code made from a file. If the file changes by one character, the code changes too.
cards.explanation: You compare the codes to see if a file was changed.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: cryptographic hashes protect the accuracy of data.

paragraphes: You get a message: “Your account is blocked. Click here to open it.” It has the logo of your bank. You feel a little afraid.
But the message is not from your bank. Someone wrote it to make you type your password on a fake website.
This trap is called phishing. The people who do this are attackers. A hacker is a person who gets into a system without permission.

decouverte.comme: A person who fishes uses bait. The fish is not forced. It chooses to bite.
decouverte.enVrai: In phishing, the message is the bait. You open the door yourself when you click. Phishing is a kind of social engineering: tricking a person to get information.

decouverte.question: A stranger calls a worker and says, “I am from IT. Tell me your password for a check.” What does a good worker do?
options: Gives the password because it is IT
Refuses and tells the security team
Gives only half of the password
decouverte.answer: Refuses and tells the security team
decouverte.explanation: A real IT team does not ask for your password. Giving half is tempting, but it still helps the attacker.

decouverte.comme: A flu virus sticks to one person and then jumps to the next. It needs a host.
decouverte.enVrai: A computer virus sticks to a file. When you open the file, it copies itself to other files. Malware is the word for every program made to cause harm. A virus is only one type. Another type is a Trojan horse: it hides inside a program that looks useful.

decouverte.comme: A thief locks your things in a chest. They give you the key only if you pay.
decouverte.enVrai: Ransomware locks your files with encryption. The attacker wants money to give you the key. You can get your files back if you pay, or if you have a copy kept somewhere else.

decouverte.texte: A ticket website gets millions of requests in one second. It cannot answer the real customers. This attack is called a denial of service (DoS). If the requests come from many computers at once, it is a distributed denial of service (DDoS).

Your credentials are your username and your password. If an attacker steals them, the attacker can sign in as you. Phishing is one way to steal them. Another way is sniffing: secretly listening to the data on a network. Spam is an unwanted message sent to many people. Some spam is phishing.

cards.question: All the files on a company computer are locked. A message asks for money to unlock them. What is this?
options: A virus that copies itself
Ransomware
Spam
A denial of service
options_why: A virus spreads from file to file. Here, the goal is to ask for money.
Spam is an unwanted message. It does not lock files.
A denial of service stops a service. It does not lock your files.
cards.answer: Ransomware
cards.explanation: Locking files in return for money is the mark of ransomware.

cards.question: A fake website asks for your password. Which attack is this?
options: Ransomware
A denial of service
Sniffing
Phishing
options_why: Ransomware locks files and asks for money.
A denial of service floods a service with requests.
Sniffing means listening to data. It does not use a fake website.
cards.answer: Phishing
cards.explanation: Phishing tries to make you give away your secret by using a trap.

cards.question: Which sentence describes malware?
options: Any program that is very old
Only a program that asks for money
Any program made to cause harm
A program that makes a computer faster
options_why: Age does not matter. Malware is defined by its goal.
That is ransomware. It is only one type of malware.
Malware does harm. It does not help.
cards.answer: Any program made to cause harm
cards.explanation: Malware is the general word. A virus, ransomware, and a Trojan horse are types of malware.

cards.question: What is a hacker?
cards.answer: A hacker is a person who tries to get into a system without the right to. This is the meaning in this course.
cards.explanation: The word sometimes means a computer expert. Here, it means the intruder.

cards.question: A worker gets an email from the “director”. He wants an urgent money transfer and says to tell nobody. What should she do FIRST?
options: Check the request in another way, like a call
Make the transfer fast so the director is not upset
Reply to the email to ask if he is sure
Send the email to the whole team
options_why: Urgency and secrecy are classic signs of a trap.
The reply may go back to the attacker.
This spreads the trap and does not check the request.
cards.answer: Check the request in another way, like a call
cards.explanation: A second trusted way to talk lets you check if the request is real.

cards.question: A worker clicked a link in a strange email. The screen looks normal. What is the BEST action?
options: Wait and see if something happens
Delete the email and say nothing
Restart the computer
Tell the security team now
options_why: Malware can work in secret. Waiting gives it more time.
The team cannot protect the others if it does not know.
Restarting does not remove a trap that may be installed.
cards.answer: Tell the security team now
cards.explanation: A quick report helps to limit the damage before it spreads.

cards.question: What is phishing?
cards.answer: Phishing is a trap message that copies a trusted sender. It pushes you to click or to give a password.
cards.explanation: The word sounds like fishing: the message is the bait.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: phishing is the most common form of social engineering.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a common sign of a phishing message?
options: It creates fear or urgency
A calm message that you expected to get
It asks for your password
The link goes to a strange website
options_why: This is a common sign. Attackers want you to act before you think.
This is a common sign. Real teams do not ask for your password.
This is a common sign. Look at where the link really goes.
cards.answer: A calm message that you expected to get
cards.explanation: A normal message that you expected is not a sign of a trap. Check the sender in any case.

cards.question: A free game hides malware inside a program that looks useful. You install it yourself. What is it?
options: A Trojan horse
A virus that copies itself
Ransomware that locks files
Spam sent to many people
options_why: A virus copies itself from file to file. This malware hides in a program.
Ransomware asks for money. Nothing here asks for money.
Spam is an unwanted message, not a hidden program.
cards.answer: A Trojan horse
cards.explanation: Like in the old story, the gift hides the danger.

cards.question: What is social engineering?
cards.answer: Tricking a person, by pretending to be someone else, to get information. Example: a fake call from the IT team.
cards.explanation: The attacker aims at the person, not at the machine.

cards.question: Which attack MOST directly stops real users from using a website?
options: Phishing messages
Credential theft by phone
A denial of service
Sniffing on a network
options_why: Phishing tricks people. It does not stop a website.
Credential theft steals sign-ins. The website still works.
Sniffing only listens. The website still works.
cards.answer: A denial of service
cards.explanation: Nothing is stolen. The service is only stopped from answering.

cards.question: Which example is the BEST case of social engineering?
options: A program locks files for money
A caller who pretends to be from the IT team
A flood of requests stops a website
A file copies itself into other files
options_why: That is ransomware, which is malware.
That is a denial of service.
That is a virus.
cards.answer: A caller who pretends to be from the IT team
cards.explanation: Social engineering tricks a person. The attacker uses words, not a program.

cards.question: What is a computer virus?
cards.answer: A virus is malware that sticks to a file and copies itself when you open that file.
cards.explanation: Like a flu virus, it needs a host to spread.

cards.question: How is a DDoS different from a DoS?
options: It steals passwords instead of stopping a service
It can only hit phones
It locks files and asks for money
The requests come from many computers at once
options_why: Both attacks aim at a service, not passwords.
It can hit any service.
That is ransomware.
cards.answer: The requests come from many computers at once
cards.explanation: Blocking one source is not enough when thousands of computers send the requests.

cards.question: An attacker secretly listens to the data on a network and reads a password. What is the attacker doing?
options: Sniffing
Phishing
Spamming
A denial of service
options_why: Phishing uses a fake message. Here the attacker only listens.
Spam is an unwanted message sent to many people.
A denial of service floods a service with requests.
cards.answer: Sniffing
cards.explanation: The listener changes nothing. They only read what passes by. Encryption stops this.

cards.question: What is ransomware?
cards.answer: Ransomware is malware that locks your files with encryption. The attacker asks for money to give you the key.
cards.explanation: A ransom is money that is demanded to set something free.

cards.question: What is credential theft?
cards.answer: Stealing a username and a password to sign in as another person. Phishing is one way to do it.
cards.explanation: With your credentials, the attacker walks in through the front door.

paragraphes: You work three hours on your homework. The computer crashes and everything is gone.
If you had a copy somewhere else, you would lose five minutes, not three hours.
This spare copy is called a backup. It is one basic defense in cybersecurity. A defense is anything that protects.

decouverte.comme: A castle has walls, guards at the gate, alarm bells, and food for a long siege.
decouverte.enVrai: A company also uses many defenses. A firewall is like the guard at the gate: it checks what goes in and out of the network. Antivirus software finds malware and removes it. Logs are written records of what happens.

decouverte.question: A flaw in a program is known. The maker sends a patch, an update that fixes the flaw. What happens if you do not install it?
options: Nothing: the flaw is harmless
The flaw stays open to attackers
The computer turns itself off
decouverte.answer: The flaw stays open to attackers
decouverte.explanation: When a flaw is known, attackers know it too. Not updating leaves a door open. “Nothing” is tempting because you see no change.

decouverte.comme: A camera at the door does not stop a theft. But later you can watch what happened.
decouverte.enVrai: Logs record who did what, and when. They do not stop an attack. They help you see it and understand it.

decouverte.texte: On Monday, a company finds that all its files are locked. It pays nothing. It has a backup from the day before, kept outside the network. In a few hours, it restores the files. To restore means to put data back from a backup. Without a backup, the company could lose years of work.

decouverte.comme: A smoke alarm rings when it sees smoke. It does not put out the fire.
decouverte.enVrai: An intrusion detection system (IDS) works like that. It sees strange behavior and warns you. It does not close the door by itself.

decouverte.titre: A spare, a test, and an incident
decouverte.texte: Redundancy means having a spare, so one failure does not stop the work. A penetration test is an attack that you allow, to find weak points before real attackers do. A security incident is an event that puts data or systems in danger.

cards.question: Which tool finds and removes malware?
options: Antivirus software
The logs of the system
A firewall for the network
A backup of the files
options_why: Logs record what happens, but they remove nothing.
A firewall filters the network. It does not clean files.
A backup keeps a copy of data. It does not remove malware.
cards.answer: Antivirus software
cards.explanation: Finding and removing malware is the job of antivirus software.

cards.question: What does a backup help you do?
options: Stop an attack before it starts
See who signed in last night
Get your data back after it is lost
Block strangers from the network
options_why: A backup blocks nothing. It helps you recover afterwards.
That is the job of logs.
That is the job of a firewall.
cards.answer: Get your data back after it is lost
cards.explanation: A backup protects against breakdowns, theft, and ransomware.

cards.question: Which defense works like a guard at the gate of a network?
options: A patch for a program
A log of the system
A backup of the files
A firewall
options_why: A patch fixes a flaw in a program.
A log is a record. It does not filter anything.
A backup is a spare copy.
cards.answer: A firewall
cards.explanation: A firewall lets data pass or blocks it, following rules.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: PCI DSS requirement 1 asks for a firewall to protect card data.

cards.question: What is a backup?
cards.answer: A backup is a copy of your data kept somewhere else, so you can get it back after a loss.
cards.explanation: It protects against breakdowns, theft, and ransomware.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: keep several copies, and keep one away from the main site.

cards.question: A company wants to recover quickly from ransomware. What is the BEST protection to have ready?
options: The newest antivirus program, and nothing else
A recent backup kept outside the network
A firewall rule that blocks all email
A log of every change in the files
options_why: Antivirus helps to prevent, but it cannot give the files back.
This stops work and does not give the files back.
Logs show what happened. They do not restore the files.
cards.answer: A recent backup kept outside the network
cards.explanation: With a good backup, the company can restore its files and refuse to pay.

cards.question: What is the MOST likely problem if the only backup is on the same computer?
options: The backup will be too small
The backup will not be possible to restore
One theft can destroy both copies
The computer will run slower
options_why: Size is not the main problem here.
The restore works. The problem is that the copy can be lost with the original.
Speed is not the main problem here.
cards.answer: One theft can destroy both copies
cards.explanation: A copy in the same place as the original does not protect against a problem that hits that place.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: keep at least one set of backups away from the main site.

cards.question: What is a firewall?
cards.answer: A firewall is a filter that lets data pass or blocks it between two networks, following rules.
cards.explanation: It works like the guard at the gate of a castle.

cards.question: A patch for a known flaw is published. What should the IT team do FIRST?
options: Test the patch first, then install it
Ignore it until an attack really happens
Wait for the yearly review
Install it on every computer right now
options_why: Waiting for an attack is reactive. The flaw is already known.
A long delay leaves the door open.
Without a test, a patch can break things.
cards.answer: Test the patch first, then install it
cards.explanation: Test first, then install quickly. Attackers also read the patch announcements.

cards.question: Which defense helps to RECOVER, NOT to prevent?
options: A firewall
A patch
Antivirus software
A backup
options_why: A firewall helps to prevent, by blocking strangers.
A patch helps to prevent, by fixing a flaw.
Antivirus helps to prevent, by finding malware.
cards.answer: A backup
cards.explanation: Before, during, after: prevent, spot, recover. A backup is for after.

cards.question: What is a patch?
cards.answer: A patch is an update that fixes a flaw in a program. Installing it is called patching.
cards.explanation: Many attacks use flaws for which a patch already exists.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: scanning and patching for weak points is good practice.

cards.question: A server log shows 1,000 failed sign-ins at three in the morning. What does this MOST likely show?
options: That the server is working in a healthy way
A possible attack that needs a look
That the firewall was removed
That the logs are broken
options_why: A thousand refused attempts at night is not a sign of good health.
Nothing in the log says this.
The logs work. They are showing the problem.
cards.answer: A possible attack that needs a look
cards.explanation: Logs help you to spot this kind of sign and react fast.

cards.question: What is the job of an intrusion detection system (IDS)?
options: To lock all the doors of the network by itself
To make copies of the files
To install the patches
To see strange behavior and warn you
options_why: An IDS warns. It does not act alone.
That is the job of a backup.
That is the job of the IT team.
cards.answer: To see strange behavior and warn you
cards.explanation: An IDS is like an alarm: it rings, but it does not close the door.

cards.question: What are logs?
cards.answer: Logs are written records of what happens in a system: who signed in, when, and what they did.
cards.explanation: They stop nothing, but they let you look into what happened.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: turn on security logs and review them to spot strange activity.

cards.question: A company hires an expert to attack its network, with permission, to find weak points. What is this BEST called?
options: A ransomware attack
A phishing attack
A penetration test of the network
A denial of service
options_why: Ransomware is a real attack. This test is allowed.
Phishing is a real trap. This test is allowed and planned.
A denial of service is a real attack that stops a service.
cards.answer: A penetration test of the network
cards.explanation: You attack yourself to find the flaws before others do.

cards.question: A company rents two internet providers. If one fails, the other works. What is this idea called?
options: Redundancy
A patch for a program
A restore of the data
A firewall for the network
options_why: A patch fixes a flaw in a program.
A restore puts data back from a backup.
A firewall filters the network.
cards.answer: Redundancy
cards.explanation: It is like a spare wheel on a car.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: doubled power, water, and internet connections.

cards.question: What does it mean to restore?
cards.answer: To restore means to put data back in place from a backup.
cards.explanation: A backup that you cannot restore is useless. You need to practice.

cards.question: What is a security incident?
cards.answer: A security incident is an event that puts data or systems in danger. Examples: ransomware, a stolen account.
cards.explanation: When an incident happens, you spot it, limit it, and then recover.

paragraphes: You leave for a vacation and forget a window open. Nobody came in yet. But a stranger walks by and looks at the window.
Three things already exist: an open window, a possible burglar, and things of value inside. The theft has not happened yet.
Experts have a word for each one. The open window is a vulnerability, a weak point. The burglar is a threat.

decouverte.comme: The open window is a weak point. The burglar is a possible danger. When the burglar really comes in, that is the burglary.
decouverte.enVrai: A vulnerability is a weak point in a system. A threat is what can use that weak point. An attack is the moment when someone really does it. An asset is anything of value that you protect, like data or people.

decouverte.question: A program has a known flaw, but nobody has used it yet. What is the flaw called?
options: A vulnerability
An attack
A virus
decouverte.explanation: The flaw is a weak point, so it is a vulnerability. Nobody used it, so there is no attack yet. “Attack” is tempting because the word sounds scary.

decouverte.comme: The sky is gray and you forgot your umbrella. Rain is possible, and you will get wet if it falls.
decouverte.enVrai: Risk is the chance that a threat uses a vulnerability and harms an asset. It depends on probability (how likely it is) and impact (how bad the damage is). With no threat or no vulnerability, the risk is lower. The image stops here: you cannot change the weather, but you can fix a vulnerability.

decouverte.texte: A worker writes a password on a paper and sticks it on the screen: that is a vulnerability. A curious visitor is a threat. If the visitor reads the password and signs in, that is an attack. The company data is the asset in danger.

A threat can also come from inside. An insider threat is a person with real access, like a worker or a partner. It can be on purpose or by mistake. A data breach is an incident where data is read or taken without permission.

cards.question: An office door does not close well. What is the door?
options: A threat from outside
An attack on the building
A risk for the company
A vulnerability
options_why: A threat is a person or event that can use the weak point.
An attack is when someone really uses the weak point.
A risk is the chance of harm. It is not the weak point itself.
cards.answer: A vulnerability
cards.explanation: The badly closed door is a weak point. The threat would be the person who uses it.

cards.question: A flood could destroy a datacenter. What is the flood?
options: A vulnerability
A threat
An asset
An attack
options_why: A vulnerability is a weak point, like having no protection against water.
An asset is what you protect, like the servers.
An attack needs someone to act on purpose. A flood is a natural event.
cards.answer: A threat
cards.explanation: A flood is a dangerous event that can hit the datacenter. It is a threat.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: floods, heat, and power failures are environmental threats.

cards.question: Which one of these is an asset?
options: The customer database
A password that is far too simple
A hacker who wants the data
A program that was never updated
options_why: That is a vulnerability. It is a weak point.
That is a threat. It is a danger.
That is a vulnerability. It is a weak point.
cards.answer: The customer database
cards.explanation: An asset is what you try to protect. Data, machines, and people are assets.

cards.question: What is a vulnerability?
cards.answer: A vulnerability is a weak point in a system that an attacker can use. Example: a program that was never updated.
cards.explanation: The vulnerability is in the system. It exists even if nobody uses it.
cards.explanation_more: Simple definition. The official definition from the manual comes later, in the galaxy about threats and risk.

cards.question: Which statement BEST describes a risk?
options: A weak point in a system that anyone can use
Anything of value that the company wants to protect
The chance that a threat harms an asset
The moment when an attacker really gets in
options_why: That is a vulnerability. A risk also needs a threat and an asset.
That is an asset. A risk is the chance of harm to it.
That is an attack. A risk is only a chance.
cards.answer: The chance that a threat harms an asset
cards.explanation: Risk sits where a threat, a vulnerability, and an asset meet.

cards.question: An attacker finds a vulnerability. Which step comes NEXT?
options: The attacker uses it, and this is the attack itself
The company suffers the damage and the loss
The vulnerability is created by the attacker
The risk becomes zero for the company
options_why: The damage comes after the attack.
The vulnerability already existed before the attacker found it.
Using a weak point makes the harm real. It does not remove the risk.
cards.answer: The attacker uses it, and this is the attack itself
cards.explanation: The chain is: a vulnerability exists, an attacker finds it, the attack, then the damage.

cards.question: What is a threat?
cards.answer: A threat is an event or a person that can cause damage. Examples: a hacker, a fire, an angry worker.
cards.explanation: The threat is not in the system. It is what can hit it.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a threat?
options: A fire in the server room of the shop
An angry former worker
A worker who makes a mistake
A program that was never updated
options_why: A fire can cause damage, so it is a threat.
A person who can cause damage is a threat.
A mistake can cause damage, so it is a threat too.
cards.answer: A program that was never updated
cards.explanation: A program that was never updated is a weak point. It is a vulnerability, not a threat.

cards.question: A company fixes every known vulnerability. What is MOST true now?
options: The risk is gone for ever
The risk is lower, but it is not zero
New threats cannot appear any more
Assets no longer need any more protection
options_why: New weak points and other threats can appear.
Threats like mistakes and breakdowns still exist.
Assets always need protection.
cards.answer: The risk is lower, but it is not zero
cards.explanation: The goal is not zero risk. The goal is to make the risk acceptable.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: the risk that remains after protection is called residual risk.

cards.question: What is an asset?
cards.answer: An asset is anything of value to an organization: people, machines, data. Example: the customer list.
cards.explanation: An asset is what you try to protect.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: an asset is anything of value.

cards.question: A scan shows a vulnerability that nobody has used yet. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Do nothing until someone really attacks it
Delete the whole system that has the flaw
Judge how likely and how bad an attack could be
Tell all the customers about the flaw today
options_why: Waiting is reactive. A threat can appear without warning.
This is an extreme action and may stop the business.
Telling everyone can help attackers. First, judge the risk.
cards.answer: Judge how likely and how bad an attack could be
cards.explanation: Evaluate before you act. Probability and impact tell you how urgent the fix is.

cards.question: Which example is the BEST case of an insider threat?
options: A stranger sends a fake email to the staff
A worker with access sends a file by mistake
A flood hits the datacenter at night
An outside website is overloaded by many requests
options_why: The stranger is outside the company.
A flood is an outside event, not a person with access.
That is a denial of service from outside.
cards.answer: A worker with access sends a file by mistake
cards.explanation: An insider threat comes from someone with real access. It can be a mistake or on purpose.

cards.question: What is a risk?
cards.answer: A risk is the chance that a threat uses a vulnerability and harms an asset. It depends on probability and impact.
cards.explanation: With no threat, or no vulnerability, the risk is lower.

cards.question: Customer names are copied by someone with no permission. What is this?
options: A data breach
A vulnerability
A denial of service
A system restore
options_why: A vulnerability is a weak point. Here, data was really taken.
A denial of service stops a service. Here, data was taken.
A restore puts data back. It is not an incident.
cards.answer: A data breach
cards.explanation: A data breach is the possible result of a successful attack.

cards.question: What does impact mean when we talk about risk?
options: How often the threat shows up
How easy the weak point is to find
How much the asset cost to buy
How bad the damage would be
options_why: That is probability.
That describes the vulnerability, not the impact.
The price of an asset is not the same as the damage.
cards.answer: How bad the damage would be
cards.explanation: Risk depends on probability and impact together.

cards.question: What is an attack?
cards.answer: An attack is the moment when someone really uses a vulnerability to cause harm.
cards.explanation: The order is: the weak point, the danger, then the action.

cards.question: What is a data breach?
cards.answer: A data breach is an incident where data is read or taken without permission. Example: a customer list that ends up online.
cards.explanation: It is the possible result of a successful attack.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: a cybercrime where information is viewed or stolen without authorization.

paragraphes: At school there are rules: no phones in class, and you carry your school planner. Other rules come from the law, like going to school being required.
A company also lives with rules from many sources: its own, its partners, and the state.
In security, you must know them all. If not, the company can pay money or lose the trust of its customers.

decouverte.comme: At home you follow your parents' rules. At school you follow the school rules. In the street you follow the law. They add up.
decouverte.enVrai: A company has its own rules, called policies. It follows standards: rules that many companies agree to use. It signs contracts with its partners. And it must obey the laws. If rules clash, the law comes first.

decouverte.question: A company does not follow a law about customer data. What can happen?
options: Nothing: a law is only advice
It can pay a fine or face a lawsuit
It only gets a bad grade
decouverte.answer: It can pay a fine or face a lawsuit
decouverte.explanation: A law must be obeyed. A fine is money that you pay for not following a law. A lawsuit is a case in court. Advice is different: it forces nobody.

decouverte.titre: The audit, like a car inspection
decouverte.comme: A car goes to an inspection. An expert checks the brakes and the lights and writes what is not good.
decouverte.enVrai: An audit is a check by a person who sees if the company follows its rules. The auditor reads documents, asks questions, and runs tests. Then the auditor writes a report. Following the rules is called compliance.

decouverte.texte: A shop keeps the name, address, and email of its customers. This is personal data: it points to one person. The shop must keep it secret. In Europe, a law lets customers ask the shop to delete their data. If the shop does not follow this law, it can pay a fine.

An organization is a group of people who work toward the same goal, like a shop or a hospital. An employee is paid by the organization. A contractor is an outside person or company that gives a service, like a technician who fixes the network. A customer buys what the organization sells.

cards.question: A technician from an outside firm repairs the network of a company. What is this person?
options: An employee of the company
A customer of the company
A contractor
An auditor who checks rules
options_why: An employee is paid by the organization itself.
A customer buys what the organization sells.
An auditor checks the rules. This person repairs the network.
cards.answer: A contractor
cards.explanation: A contractor is an outsider who gives a service. They may see company data, so a contract must frame their work.

cards.question: Which sentence about a law is true?
options: A law is advice that companies may skip
A law must be obeyed by everyone it covers
A law is a rule that one company writes for itself
A law is a deal between two companies
options_why: A law is required. Not following it can cost a fine.
That is a policy. A law comes from the state.
That is a contract. A law applies to everyone.
cards.answer: A law must be obeyed by everyone it covers
cards.explanation: A law comes from the state and applies to everyone in the country.

cards.question: What is an audit?
options: A check that the organization follows its rules
A written deal between two companies
A set of rules that many companies choose to follow
A sum of money paid for breaking a law
options_why: That is a contract.
That is a standard.
That is a fine.
cards.answer: A check that the organization follows its rules
cards.explanation: The auditor reads documents, asks questions, and runs tests. Then they write a report.

cards.question: What is a policy?
cards.answer: A policy is an instruction that an organization gives to its workers. Example: lock your screen when you leave.
cards.explanation: A policy is a rule that the company writes for itself.
